title: “He gathereth the waters of the sea together as an heap” — the Greek has “as in a wineskin”
summary: The KJV has God gather the sea waters “as an heap”. The Septuagint, in Brenton’s Greek, has ὡσεὶ ἀσκόν, “as in a wineskin”.
text:
Preserved draft text:
KJV Psalm 33:7: “He gathereth the waters of the sea together as an heap: he layeth up the depth in storehouses.” Hebrew (WLC) Psalm 33:7: כֹּנֵ֣ס כַּ֭נֵּד מֵ֣י הַיָּ֑ם נֹתֵ֖ן בְּאֹצָרֹ֣ות תְּהֹומֹֽות׃ Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Psalm 32:7: Συνάγων ὡσεὶ ἀσκὸν ὕδατα θαλάσσης, τιθεὶς ἐν θησαυροῖς ἀβύσσους. [Gathering the waters of the sea as in a wineskin, putting abysses in storehouses.] Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/19/33/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/PSA032.htm.

New draft supplemental text (reported, unverified):
KJV Psalms 33:7: “He gathereth the waters of the sea together as an heap: he layeth up the depth in storehouses.” Hebrew (WLC) 33:7: כֹּנֵ֣ס כַּ֭נֵּד מֵ֣י הַיָּ֑ם נֹתֵ֖ן בְּאֹצָרֹ֣ות תְּהֹומֹֽות׃. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 32:7: Συνάγων ὡσεὶ ἀσκὸν ὕδατα θαλάσσης, τιθεὶς ἐν θησαυροῖς ἀβύσσους. [Gathering the waters of the sea as a wineskin, putting the deeps in storehouses]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/19/33/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/PSA032.htm.
reasoning:
Preserved draft reasoning:
A heap is a pile of water standing up, and a wineskin is a bag that holds it. The KJV has the former. The Greek has ὡσεὶ ἀσκὸν. The Hebrew has כַּ֭נֵּד in that slot, and the KJV reading follows it. The two English pictures differ: waters piled up against a limit, or waters held inside a container.

New draft supplemental reasoning (reported, unverified):
A heap is a pile of the waters standing on one another. A skin bottle is a vessel that holds them. The Greek ἀσκός is the word for a leather bag or wineskin, and Brenton’s English prints “bottle”. The two texts give two pictures of how the sea is gathered, as a mound in the KJV and as the contents of a container in the Greek.
scope:
Preserved draft scope:
T applies at 33:7 and only to this noun; the Greek and the KJV agree on the rest of the verse (gathering the sea, storing the deeps). The Hebrew is quoted so that the three texts stand together; this record does not say what the Hebrew word means or that “heap” is wrong. The difference found is between the KJV and the Greek. This compares the wording of three texts and does not show which is original. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. The Greek is Brenton's printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. New draft supplemental scope (reported, unverified):
T applies at Psalm 33:7 (Greek 32:7) and only to the image of the gathering; both texts have God gathering the sea’s waters and laying up the deeps in storehouses. The record does not decide how the Hebrew word כַּנֵּד should be read; it quotes the Hebrew so that the three texts stand together. title: “They looked, but there was none to save” — the Greek of 2 Samuel 22:42 has “they will cry”
summary: The KJV and the Hebrew of 2 Samuel 22:42 say the enemies “looked” (יִשְׁעוּ) but there was none to save. Brenton’s Greek of 2 Samuel 22:42 reads Βοήσονται, “they will cry”, as Brenton’s Greek of Psalm 17:42 (KJV Psalm 18:41) reads Ἐκέκραξαν, “they cried”.
text: KJV Psalm 18:41: “They cried, but there was none to save them: even unto the Lord, but he answered them not.” KJV 2 Samuel 22:42: “They looked, but there was none to save; even unto the Lord, but he answered them not.” Hebrew (WLC) Psalm 18:42: יְשַׁוְּע֥וּ וְאֵין־מֹושִׁ֑יעַ עַל־יְ֝הוָ֗ה וְלֹ֣א עָנָֽם׃ Hebrew (WLC) 2 Samuel 22:42: יִשְׁע֖וּ וְאֵ֣ין מֹשִׁ֑יעַ אֶל־יְהוָ֖ה וְלֹ֥א עָנָֽם׃ Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Psalm 17:42: Ἐκέκραξαν, καὶ οὐκ ἦν ὁ σώζων· πρὸς Κύριον, καὶ οὐκ εἰσήκουεν αὐτῶν. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 2 Samuel 22:42: Βοήσονται, καὶ οὐκ ἔστι βοηθὸς, πρὸς Κύριον, καὶ οὐκ ἐπήκουσεν αὐτῶν. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/19/18/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/10/22/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/PSA017.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2SA22.htm.
reasoning: Brenton’s Greek of 2 Samuel 22:42 says “they will cry”, where the KJV and Hebrew say “looked”. The Psalm supplies context, not a separate finding.
scope: T applies at 2 Samuel 22:42, Septuagint only. The KJV agrees with the Hebrew. Psalm 18:41 is context and carries no tag.

title: “He is the tower of salvation for his king” — the Greek of 2 Samuel 22:51 has “magnifying the salvations of his king”
summary: The KJV of 2 Samuel 22:51 reads “He is the tower of salvation for his king”. Brenton’s Greek of 2 Samuel 22:51 reads Μεγαλύνων τὰς σωτηρίας βασιλέως αὐτοῦ, “magnifying the salvations of his king”, as Brenton’s Greek of Psalm 17:51 does. The Hebrew text carries a written form and a read form of the first word in both books; the KJV follows the read form in each, and that notation is background only.
text: KJV Psalm 18:50: “Great deliverance giveth he to his king; and sheweth mercy to his anointed, to David, and to his seed for evermore.” KJV 2 Samuel 22:51: “He is the tower of salvation for his king: and sheweth mercy to his anointed, unto David, and to his seed for evermore.” Hebrew (WLC) Psalm 18:51: [מִגְדֹּל כ] (מַגְדִּיל֮ ק) יְשׁוּעֹ֪ות מַ֫לְכֹּ֥ו וְעֹ֤שֶׂה חֶ֨סֶד ׀ לִמְשִׁיחֹ֗ו לְדָוִ֥ד וּלְזַרְעֹ֗ו עַד־עֹולָֽם׃ Hebrew (WLC) 2 Samuel 22:51: [מִגְדִיל כ] (מִגְדֹּ֖ול ק) יְשׁוּעֹ֣ות מַלְכֹּ֑ו וְעֹֽשֶׂה־חֶ֧סֶד לִמְשִׁיחֹ֛ו לְדָוִ֥ד וּלְזַרְעֹ֖ו עַד־עֹולָֽם׃ ף Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Psalm 17:51: Μεγαλύνων τὰς σωτηρίας τοῦ βασιλέως αὐτοῦ, καὶ ποιῶν ἔλεος τῷ χριστῷ αὐτοῦ τῷ Δαυὶδ, καὶ τῷ σπέρματι αὐτοῦ ἕως αἰῶνος. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 2 Samuel 22:51: Μεγαλύνων τὰς σωτηρίας βασιλέως αὐτοῦ, καὶ ποιῶν ἔλεος τῷ χριστῷ αὐτοῦ τῷ Δαυὶδ, καὶ τῷ σπέρματι αὐτοῦ ἕως αἰῶνος. Καὶ οὗτοι οἱ λόγοι Δαυὶδ οἱ ἔσχατοι· Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/19/18/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/10/22/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/PSA017.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/2SA22.htm.

title: “Slay them not” (Psalm 59:11) — “Consume them in wrath, consume them, that they may not be” (59:13)
summary: In one prayer the speaker asks that his enemies not be slain, lest his people forget, and two verses later asks that they be consumed so that they are no more.
text: KJV Psalm 59:11: “Slay them not, lest my people forget: scatter them by thy power; and bring them down, O Lord our shield.” KJV Psalm 59:13: “Consume them in wrath, consume them, that they may not be: and let them know that God ruleth in Jacob unto the ends of the earth. Selah.” Hebrew (WLC) Psalm 59:12: אַל־תַּהַרְגֵ֤ם ׀ פֶּֽן־יִשְׁכְּח֬וּ עַמִּ֗י הֲנִיעֵ֣מֹו בְ֭חֵילְךָ וְהֹורִידֵ֑מֹו מָֽגִנֵּ֣נוּ אֲדֹנָֽי׃ Hebrew (WLC) Psalm 59:14: כַּלֵּ֥ה בְחֵמָה֮ כַּלֵּ֪ה וְֽאֵ֫ינֵ֥מֹו וְֽיֵדְע֗וּ כִּֽי־אֱ֭לֹהִים מֹשֵׁ֣ל בְּיַעֲקֹ֑ב לְאַפְסֵ֖י הָאָ֣רֶץ סֶֽלָה׃ Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Psalm 58:12: Μὴ ἀποκτείνῃς αὐτοὺς, μήποτε ἐπιλάθωνται τοῦ νόμου σου· διασκόρπισον αὐτοὺς ἐν τῇ δυνάμει σου, καὶ κατάγαγε αὐτοὺς ὁ ὑπερασπιστής μου Κύριε. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Psalm 58:14: συντέλειαι, ἐν ὀργῇ συντελείας, καὶ οὐ μὴ ὑπάρξουσι· καὶ γνώσονται ὅτι ὁ Θεὸς τοῦ Ἰακὼβ δεσπόζει τῶν περάτων τῆς γῆς· διάψαλμα. Fetched from https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/PSA059.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/19/59/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/PSA058.htm.
reasoning: Verse 11 asks that the enemies not be killed, giving a reason (so that the people do not forget) and asking instead that they be scattered and brought down. Verse 13 asks that they be consumed in wrath until they are not. The Hebrew keeps the contrast: אַל־תַּהַרְגֵ֤ (do not kill them) and כַּלֵּ֥ה twice (finish, consume) with וְֽאֵ֫ינֵ֥מֹו (and they are not). The Greek has Μὴ ἀποκτείνῃς αὐτοὺς (do not kill them) and καὶ οὐ μὴ ὑπάρξουσι (and they shall not exist). The KJV and Hebrew juxtapose requests to spare and to consume. The Greek also juxtaposes not killing and destruction, but its destruction clause is not grammatically identical to the Hebrew imperatives. This does not establish inconsistent intentions.
scope: This sets two requests of one prayer beside each other in the KJV, the Hebrew and the Greek. It does not say the psalm contradicts itself or that the writer was inconsistent. The two verses may be read as two stages (scattering now, consuming later), or “not be” may mean their power or standing rather than their lives; the psalm does not say which. Both are the speaker’s prayers, not statements about what God does. The verses are poetry and the comparison is of the words printed. This record compares the requests in verses 11 and 13; it does not claim that the KJV, Hebrew and Greek agree in all details. Greek 58:12 has “your law” where Hebrew 59:12/KJV 59:11 has “my people”; the separate translation finding retains Brenton’s variant note. title: “Sore broken us in the place of dragons” — the Greek has “a place of affliction”
summary: In the KJV the speakers say God has sore broken them “in the place of dragons”. The Septuagint, in Brenton’s Greek, has ἐν τόπῳ κακώσεως, “in a place of affliction”, where the KJV has “dragons”.
text: KJV Psalm 44:19: “Though thou hast sore broken us in the place of dragons, and covered us with the shadow of death.” Hebrew (WLC) Psalm 44:20: כִּ֣י דִ֭כִּיתָנוּ בִּמְקֹ֣ום תַּנִּ֑ים וַתְּכַ֖ס עָלֵ֣ינוּ בְצַלְמָֽוֶת׃ Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Psalm 43:20: Ὅτι ἐταπείνωσας ἡμᾶς ἐν τόπῳ κακώσεως, καὶ ἐπεκάλυψεν ἡμᾶς σκιὰ θανάτου. [Because you humbled us in a place of affliction, and the shadow of death covered us.] Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/19/44/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/PSA043.htm.
reasoning: Both texts name the place where the people were crushed or brought low. The KJV names it “the place of dragons”, a place where creatures live. The Greek names it τόπῳ κακώσεως, a place of affliction or ill-treatment, which names a condition and not a creature. The Hebrew has תַּנִּ֑ים in the same slot, and the KJV reading follows it. A reader of the English pictures a lair of creatures; a reader of the Greek pictures a place of suffering.
scope: T applies at 44:19 and only to the noun; the rest of the verse (the shadow of death covering them) agrees. The difference found is between the KJV and the Greek. The Hebrew is quoted so that the three texts stand together; this record does not say what the Hebrew word means, and does not say that “dragons” is wrong. The Greek verb of the first half (ἐταπείνωσας, “you humbled”) also differs from the KJV “sore broken”; it is not tagged separately. A published record on Job 30:29 notes a comparable Greek reading for a similar Hebrew noun. This compares the wording of three texts and does not show which is original. title: “He will be our guide even unto death” — the Greek has “for the ages”
summary: The KJV ends the psalm “he will be our guide even unto death”. The Septuagint, in Brenton’s Greek, ends with αὐτὸς ποιμανεῖ ἡμᾶς εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας, “he will shepherd us to the ages”.
text: KJV Psalm 48:14: “For this God is our God for ever and ever: he will be our guide even unto death.” Hebrew (WLC) Psalm 48:15: כִּ֤י זֶ֨ה ׀ אֱלֹהִ֣ים אֱ֭לֹהֵינוּ עֹולָ֣ם וָעֶ֑ד ה֖וּא יְנַהֲגֵ֣נוּ עַל־מֽוּת׃ Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Psalm 47:15: Ὅτι οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα καὶ εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τοῦ αἰῶνος, αὐτὸς ποιμανεῖ ἡμᾶς εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας. reasoning: The KJV sets an end point, death, to the guiding. The Greek has εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας (to the ages), which has no end point. The Hebrew closes with עַל־מֽוּת, and the KJV reading follows it. A reader of the English is told God guides his people until they die; a reader of the Greek is told he will shepherd them without end.

title: “That seek thy face, O Jacob” — the Greek has “the face of the God of Jacob”
summary: In the KJV the seekers are addressed as “Jacob”, and the face they seek is “thy face”. The Septuagint, in Brenton’s Greek, has them seek τὸ πρόσωπον τοῦ Θεοῦ Ἰακώβ, “the face of the God of Jacob”.
text: KJV Psalm 24:6: “This is the generation of them that seek him, that seek thy face, O Jacob. Selah.” Hebrew (WLC) Psalm 24:6: זֶ֭ה דֹּ֣ור [דֹּרְשֹׁו כ] (דֹּרְשָׁ֑יו ק) מְבַקְשֵׁ֨י פָנֶ֖יךָ יַעֲקֹ֣ב סֶֽלָה׃ Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Psalm 23:6: Αὕτη ἡ γενεὰ ζητούντων αὐτὸν, ζητούντων τὸ πρόσωπον τοῦ Θεοῦ Ἰακώβ. διάψαλμα. title: “Save, Lord: let the king hear us when we call” — the Greek asks the Lord to save the king
summary: The KJV ends the psalm with a call to the Lord to save, and then asks that the king hear us. The Septuagint, in Brenton’s Greek, asks the Lord to save the king and to hear us; the king is the one saved, not the one who hears.
text: KJV Psalms 20:9: “Save, Lord: let the king hear us when we call.” Hebrew (WLC) 20:10: יְהוָ֥ה הֹושִׁ֑יעָה הַ֝מֶּ֗לֶךְ יַעֲנֵ֥נוּ בְיֹום־קָרְאֵֽנוּ׃. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 19:10: Κύριε σῶσον τὸν βασιλέα καὶ ἐπάκουσον ἡμῶν, ἐν ᾗ ἂν ἡμέρᾳ ἐπικαλεσώμεθά σε. [Lord, save the king, and hear us on whatever day we call upon you]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/19/20/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/PSA019.htm.
reasoning: In the KJV the king is the subject of the second clause: “let the king hear us when we call”. In the Greek the king is the object of the first clause, σῶσον τὸν βασιλέα, “save the king”, and the one who hears is the same Lord who is addressed: ἐπάκουσον ἡμῶν, “hear us”. The two verses therefore name different people as the one who hears the prayer, and they give the king a different place in the line, as the one acted upon in the Greek and as the one who hears in the KJV.

title: “O ye seed of Israel his servant” (1 Chronicles 16:13) and “O ye seed of Abraham his servant” (Psalm 105:6)
summary: David’s song in 1 Chronicles 16 and Psalm 105 share their opening verses. 1 Chronicles 16:13 addresses the seed of Israel, God’s servant; Psalm 105:6 addresses the seed of Abraham, God’s servant.
text: KJV 1 Chronicles 16:13: “O ye seed of Israel his servant, ye children of Jacob, his chosen ones.” Hebrew (WLC) 1 Chronicles 16:13: זֶ֚רַע יִשְׂרָאֵ֣ל עַבְדֹּ֔ו בְּנֵ֥י יַעֲקֹ֖ב בְּחִירָֽיו׃. KJV Psalm 105:6: “O ye seed of Abraham his servant, ye children of Jacob his chosen.” Hebrew (WLC) Psalm 105:6: זֶ֭רַע אַבְרָהָ֣ם עַבְדֹּ֑ו בְּנֵ֖י יַעֲקֹ֣ב בְּחִירָֽיו׃. Fetched from https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/1CH16.htm and https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/PSA105.htm and https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/13/16/ and https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/19/105/.
reasoning: The two verses are the same verse except for the first name. Israel is another name for Jacob, so 1 Chronicles 16:13 and its second half, “children of Jacob”, name the same man twice in two forms. Psalm 105:6 names Abraham first and Jacob second. The seed addressed is therefore the seed of Israel in one book and the seed of Abraham in the other; Abraham is Jacob’s grandfather and a wider seed.
scope: This sets the same verse in two books beside each other as the KJV gives them. It does not say either book is wrong: the same song may have been written down in two forms, and the books do not say which came first. 1 Chronicles 16:7 introduces the song as one David delivered to Asaph and his brethren. The other differences between the two copies of the song are not recorded here. Only the KJV and the Hebrew wording of the verses were compared. title: “Strength and gladness are in his place” (1 Chronicles 16:27) and “strength and beauty are in his sanctuary” (Psalm 96:6)
summary: David’s song in 1 Chronicles 16 and Psalm 96 share this verse. 1 Chronicles 16:27 has “strength and gladness” (עֹז וְחֶדְוָה) “in his place” (בִּמְקוֹמוֹ); Psalm 96:6 has “strength and beauty” (עֹז וְתִפְאֶרֶת) “in his sanctuary” (בְּמִקְדָּשׁוֹ). The first pair, “glory and honour” and “honour and majesty”, is the same Hebrew pair (הוֹד וְהָדָר) in both and is not a difference.
text: KJV 1 Chronicles 16:27: “Glory and honour are in his presence; strength and gladness are in his place.” Hebrew (WLC) 1 Chronicles 16:27: הֹ֤וד וְהָדָר֙ לְפָנָ֔יו עֹ֥ז וְחֶדְוָ֖ה בִּמְקֹמֹֽו׃. KJV Psalm 96:6: “Honour and majesty are before him: strength and beauty are in his sanctuary.” Hebrew (WLC) Psalm 96:6: הֹוד־וְהָדָ֥ר לְפָנָ֑יו עֹ֥ז וְ֝תִפְאֶ֗רֶת בְּמִקְדָּשֹֽׁו׃. reasoning: The first pair is “glory and honour” (הוֹד וְהָדָר) in 1 Chronicles, and in Psalm 96 the Hebrew has the same two words and the KJV prints them “honour and majesty”. The second pair is “strength and gladness” (עֹז וְחֶדְוָה) in 1 Chronicles and “strength and beauty” (עֹז וְתִפְאֶרֶת) in Psalm 96. The place is “his place” (בִּמְקוֹמוֹ) in one and “his sanctuary” (בְּמִקְדָּשׁוֹ) in the other. Gladness and beauty, and a place and a sanctuary, are different things.
scope: This sets the same verse in two books beside each other as the KJV gives them. It does not say either book is wrong, or which came first; the first pair of Hebrew words is the same and only the KJV’s English differs there, and that is not claimed as a difference of meaning.
